title: Authentication and identity boundaries in a full-stack app
description: Separate session loading, signed-out state, route guards, and server authorization. A guide adapted from the supplied Grok authentication documentation.
sections: Start with the session state

A session lookup has at least three useful outcomes: unresolved, authenticated, and unauthenticated. A null user value may represent either loading or a completed lookup that found no session. Redirecting on null alone can bounce an authenticated visitor during a reload. The supplied template distinguishes user data from a pending flag; preserve that distinction in any adaptation.
UI gates and authorization

An interface gate controls what the visitor sees. It does not authorize a server operation. Check the resolved identity and resource ownership inside the operation that reads or changes protected data. Do not trust a user identifier supplied in a request body as the caller identity. Rendering a signed-in component is useful for presentation, but a direct request must cross the same authorization boundary.
Avoid authentication flicker

Wait until the session check finishes before rendering a sign-in call to action. A loading skeleton or neutral state can communicate progress without falsely declaring that the user is signed out. A data-source outage should have its own error state; it should not be converted into a login requirement merely because the fetch failed.
OAuth and account ownership

OAuth redirects, callback verification, cookies, and session creation belong to the chosen identity implementation. Review its current official documentation before copying a template helper. The supplied platform documentation describes platform-managed identity behavior; those helpers are not a portable OAuth server and are not installed by this static portfolio.
Checks before release

Test a signed-out visitor, a valid session, an expired session, and a delayed session lookup. Then issue a direct request for another user's resource. Confirm that the operation rejects the request even if the client interface is bypassed. Keep test credentials synthetic and redact tokens from failure output.
Scope of the example

This article explains the supplied template's boundaries. It does not claim that this portfolio has authentication or that an OAuth integration was executed. The portfolio is static; authentication belongs in a separate application with a reviewed backend.

title: PostgreSQL persistence and local preview boundaries
description: Understand the supplied Neon and PGLite integration, server-only access, migrations, ownership checks, and deployment persistence.
sections: Choose persistence deliberately

The supplied template offers PostgreSQL-backed persistence with a local embedded fallback. A browser-local preference does not need a shared database. Records that must survive across devices or be shared between users do. Make that requirement explicit before introducing migrations and operational dependencies.
Preview is a different environment

The local PGLite fallback can make a preview work without a provisioned remote database. That is useful for development, but successful preview writes do not establish deployed durability. Record which database source the application is using, and confirm that a production restart preserves a synthetic record.
Keep access on the server

The supplied database helper belongs in server functions or server loaders. A database connection string is a server credential and should not appear in client bundles or API responses. Put schema changes in migrations with a deliberate order, and keep query values parameterized rather than building SQL by concatenating user input.
Ownership is part of the query

For user-owned records, obtain the caller identity from the session and enforce it in reads and writes. A correctly parameterized query can still disclose another user's data when the ownership condition is absent. Test that a guessed resource identifier cannot cross the tenant boundary.
Plan failure and recovery

Connection availability, migration compatibility, and backup restoration are separate concerns. An application that can write one row may still fail during a dependency outage or upgrade. Test an unavailable database and preserve an explicit error state. Restore a backup into an isolated instance before describing the installation as recoverable.
Validate the deployed mode

Use synthetic data to test write, read, restart, and read again. Inspect the documented provisioning switch in the actual platform instead of assuming the presence of migration files selects the correct backend. The static portfolio includes no database; this guide is an adaptation of the supplied platform documentation.

title: WebRTC data channels and the trust boundary of peer-to-peer play
description: A practical design guide to signaling, mesh growth, peer authority, privacy, connection failures, and lifecycle cleanup.
sections: Separate signaling from gameplay

WebRTC peers exchange connection information through signaling, then establish a data channel under the network conditions available to them. The supplied template describes a mesh primitive and a small signaling route to implement. A signaling endpoint does not itself provide authoritative game-state validation.
Count the connections

In a full mesh, each participant connects to every other participant. The number of peer pairs is n times n minus one divided by two: four participants need six pairs, while eight need twenty-eight. Room size affects connection management and upload demand. Measure the actual payload rate before choosing a capacity limit.
Choose the authority model

A peer can modify its client and send false positions or scores. Cooperative play among known participants has different requirements from competitive ranking. If the product requires trusted results, define an authoritative validation path rather than accepting peer messages as proof of fair play.
Make connection failures visible

NAT and firewall behavior can prevent direct connectivity. Applications may require relay infrastructure depending on their design. The supplied template's failure state should be surfaced per peer; do not leave a participant in a permanent connecting state. This article makes no measured latency or connection-success claim.
Handle lifecycle and privacy

Leaving a room should close data channels, release listeners, and stop retry activity. Reconnect behavior needs stable participant identity and a clear rule for stale messages. Peer connectivity can expose network information to participants, so explain the product's privacy boundary before matchmaking with strangers.
Test a small room

Connect two test clients, send ordered state updates, disconnect one participant, and inspect recovery. Repeat with a third participant and verify that a departing peer does not leave ghost state. Introduce a forged score message to confirm that the chosen authority model handles it as intended. These are proposed checks, not reported results.

title: Browser game loops: timing, input, and explicit state
description: Turn a game prototype into a inspectable interaction loop with bounded timing, focus handling, state transitions, and restart behavior.
sections: Separate simulation from rendering

A game loop samples input, advances state, and renders the current view. These responsibilities can be implemented together initially, but their boundaries matter during testing. Rendering frequency may vary with device load or a background tab; a simulation should not assume every frame has the same duration.
Make the state machine visible

Use explicit states such as ready, playing, paused, and finished. Define which actions are accepted in each state. Restart should initialize the same resources and values as a fresh start. A collection of loosely related boolean flags can allow impossible combinations that become difficult to reproduce.
Input has a lifecycle

Track key down and key up consistently, and clear held input when the page loses focus. A missed key-up event can leave a character moving after the player returns to the tab. Touch controls need equivalent actions rather than relying on a keyboard-only workflow.
Bound timing changes

Choose a deliberate timing strategy and handle unusually long frame gaps. A large delta after suspension can move an object through a collision boundary in one update. Test paused tabs and slow devices before deciding whether to clamp elapsed time, use fixed simulation steps, or reset the accumulator on resume.
Design the first useful minute

Tell the player the objective and show the controls before demanding a precise action. Keep retry fast and make win and loss states distinguishable. The supplied game documentation covers several engines and genres; choose one coherent loop instead of combining every available subsystem.
Review restart and cleanup

Start, pause, resume, finish, and restart repeatedly. Check listener counts, timers, audio, and memory growth. Use a small deterministic scenario to reproduce a collision or scoring error. This article is design guidance adapted from the supplied game documentation; the portfolio does not run a game engine.

title: Three.js scene lifecycle in a React application
description: Manage rendering, sizing, resources, and teardown when embedding a Three.js scene inside a component-based application.
sections: Use one dependency strategy

The supplied reference describes a component-based application with package imports. Do not mix an old CDN release, a different installed release, and examples from an unrelated API version. Record the dependency version and check its official documentation before choosing loaders, renderer options, or material APIs.
Treat the scene as an owned resource

A scene integration creates resources such as a canvas, renderer, animation loop, geometries, materials, and textures. Give them a lifecycle owner. React component teardown should stop the loop and detach listeners. Removing a DOM element does not automatically dispose every graphics resource.
Size for the actual container

Use the container's available dimensions when updating the renderer and camera aspect ratio. A full-window assumption fails inside a dashboard panel or responsive card. High device-pixel ratios can increase rendering demand; choose a deliberate budget and compare visual quality with observed performance.
Handle load and failure states

A model or texture request can fail or take longer than expected. Show a useful loading state and a readable fallback. Avoid rendering an empty black panel that suggests the entire interface is broken. The surrounding controls should remain usable while assets load.
Respect the product's interaction model

A decorative scene should not intercept scrolling or keyboard input needed by the page. An interactive scene needs visible controls and an explanation of what the user can do. Provide a static or textual path for content that must remain accessible without a working graphics context.
Verify teardown and remounting

Mount and unmount the scene repeatedly, resize its container, and simulate an asset failure. Inspect whether animation continues after teardown or listeners accumulate. The supplied documentation includes an official Three.js reference pack; this article summarizes integration boundaries without claiming that its examples were rendered or benchmarked.

title: A server-side LLM client with explicit cost and failure boundaries
description: Keep model credentials on the server, validate requests, bound generation, and preserve unavailable and partial-response states.
sections: Keep credentials behind the server boundary

The supplied platform documentation describes a server-injected model API credential. Read it only in server code and never expose it through a client-prefixed variable, response body, or log. A browser calling your server does not need to know the provider credential.
Validate before spending

A model request can consume the owner's quota. Validate the intended operation, input size, and permission before making the provider call. Public endpoints need a usage policy appropriate to the application. A polished button should not hide an unbounded generation loop or automatic repeat calls.
Choose versions from current documentation

Provider model names, endpoints, and supported features change. The supplied platform snapshot is an integration reference, not a live model catalog. Verify the selected model and request shape against the provider's current official documentation. Record the configuration used for any later measurement.
Treat missing configuration as a real state

When the credential is absent or the backend is unavailable, surface an unavailable state. Do not return a fabricated model answer to keep the interface looking complete. Distinguish configuration failure, request validation failure, timeout, and provider rejection so operators can act on the actual problem.
Streaming needs completion semantics

A stream can contain useful partial output and still fail before the operation finishes. Track completion separately from text arrival. Handle cancellation and client disconnects, and decide what generated artifacts survive. If a response triggers a tool action, validate that action through a separate authorization boundary.
Test the inexpensive paths first

Test missing configuration and invalid input without a provider call. Use an explicit budget for a valid integration check, record the selected model, and preserve the observed response status. This static portfolio makes no model API calls; the guide describes the server-side boundary from the supplied integration documentation.

title: A small design system: tokens, states, and accessible composition
description: Build a consistent interface from reusable tokens and explicit interaction states, with responsive reading and keyboard access.
sections: Define the vocabulary once

A small design system starts with a palette, type scale, spacing rhythm, radii, and component states. Store these decisions in shared tokens so a theme change updates the whole interface. Repeating unrelated values across components makes visual drift hard to diagnose.
Design around the reader's task

Hierarchy should make the next useful action apparent. An engineering portfolio benefits from readable project boundaries, direct source links, and a connected reading path. Decorative status indicators should not imply that code ran or that a capability was verified.
States are part of the component

A button needs more than a normal appearance. Define focus, disabled, pending, and error behavior where those states apply. A form should preserve the user's input after a recoverable failure. A missing backend should have an explicit unavailable state rather than a permanently spinning loader.
Use contrast and focus deliberately

Check text and controls against their actual backgrounds in each theme. Focus indicators should remain visible for keyboard users. Labels should communicate meaning without depending on color alone. Automated checks can find some issues, but a full accessibility claim needs broader interaction and assistive-technology review.
Compose for narrow screens

Let layouts reduce column count and keep text readable before adding complicated navigation. Code blocks need a bounded horizontal scroll area so they do not widen the entire page. Check long titles, lengthy URLs, and expanded details panels on a narrow viewport.
Motion should support interaction

Use restrained transitions to show relationships or state changes. Respect reduced-motion preferences and avoid continuously animated decoration that competes with reading. The supplied design reference provides a broader system; this guide adapts its token and composition principles without claiming a formal accessibility certification.
